claims.statement: Users can understand unfamiliar tabular data through one connected workspace of field summaries, source rows, charts, and filters.
Useful tables and charts appear from field types and data distributions with few required choices.
Table controls adapt to row count, column count, field type, and the user's task.
Sorting, filtering, visible columns, formatting, detail disclosure, and export work as one coherent table experience.
Chart brushing, table filters, and explicit filter controls update related views through shared active-row state.
The workspace makes active filters, filter scope, remaining rows, and reset behavior clear.
Saved state restores charts, layout, calculations, filters, formats, and other settings needed to reproduce an analysis.
Faceted views support direct comparison through deliberate shared scales, legends, headers, and interaction behavior.
A chart definition can describe its full path from source data through transformations and rendering.
Users can trace a rendered mark back to contributing rows and intermediate transformations.
The data model can eventually represent multiple tables, relationships, joins, lookups, aggregations, and derived values.
Small or known-schema tables do not expose advanced controls without a concrete user need.
Charts do not hide material data transformations inside opaque rendering code.
Agents may create deterministic dashboards through a thin specification rather than generated component code.
Byron is the primary consumer, and his complete analysis application decides near-term product priorities.
Other React developers can mount the complete analysis workspace with supplied rows and optional configuration or state.
The primary application consumes the same public package boundary offered to other developers.
Breaking public API changes are acceptable, and backward compatibility is not required during current development.
The first major program boundary assumes one data source and defers multiple sources and joins.
The demo includes small purposeful datasets that make source inspection and chart exploration pleasant.
The public component accepts one in-memory row array and optional saved workspace state.
Shared cross-filtering, calculations, a resizable grid, saved state, faceting, and eleven registered view types already exist.
The table supports basic column choice, paging, sorting, text filters, search, width changes, and CSV export.
The table lacks grouping, row selection, virtual scrolling, column reordering, rich cells, distributions, and type-aware filters.
The chart model uses per-type settings and renderers rather than one composable source-to-glyph specification.
The demo already consumes the package's public main entry point instead of importing internal workspace code.
The main component accepts data and initial saved state but exposes no public state-change callback for host persistence.
The repository has several large random samples, but their unseeded generation and generic fields make them weak default examples.

package_boundary.compatibility: breaking changes allowed during current development

conflicts.summary: The transcripts describe an end-user workspace, while the repository presents a reusable React package plus demo.
conflicts.resolution: Resolved: the application is primary, while the package owns the reusable analysis workspace and remains its public engine.

conflicts.summary: Multiple tables are a repeated long-term goal, but the current API and implementation assume one row array.
conflicts.resolution: Resolved: keep multiple tables as an eventual goal and use one source for the first major program boundary.

shape.appetite: One focused vertical slice delivered through several small waves, with one in-memory data source.
shape.problem: A user can load data and create charts, but the first exploration loop is fragmented and under-explained.

recommended_shape.summary: Use a small dataset pack and one shared field profile to drive a default field summary, improved source table, type-aware filters, and chart defaults inside the public package. Keep source ownership and persistence in the host application.
recommended_shape.public_boundary: The application supplies rows and optional saved state. The package owns the analysis workspace and emits serializable state changes.
dataset_pack: Palmer Penguins for mixed values, groups, and missing data
UCI red wine quality for numeric distributions and correlations
a deterministic synthetic shop operations fixture for dates, booleans, nulls, skew, seasonality, and outliers
the existing Lorenz fixture for linked selection and faceting
provisional_choices: which field actions appear in the first summary

success_moves: Prove the complete flow through the package's public entry point in the demo.
Use one field profile across summary, table, filters, and later chart defaults.
Keep storage outside the package and expose one small state-emission seam.
Improve numeric, categorical, text, and date behavior in separate useful steps.
Measure a representative dataset before adding table virtualization.
Keep tests focused on profiling, filtering, and serialization logic. Give each small dataset one clear behavior to prove.

first_proof.question: Can the public package turn one arbitrary dataset into a clear, stateful exploration loop without application-specific analysis code?
first_proof.artifact: A demo flow with Palmer Penguins and a deterministic synthetic shop fixture, default field summary and source table, numeric and categorical filters, visible active-row state, and host state capture.
first_proof.decision_rule: Proceed when summary, table, and one chart agree on types, filters, and remaining rows, and reload restores the analysis through the public API.

milestones.title: Loaded rows become an inspection workspace
milestones.outcome: Rows loaded without saved state show a shared field summary and source table by default.
milestones.proof: Palmer Penguins and shop operations open through the public package with correct field and row facts.
milestones.valid_intermediate_state: Uploads and new consumers get useful inspection views without filter or persistence changes.
milestones.rollback: Revert the default workspace and shared profile changes; existing saved examples remain available.
milestones.proof_evidence: Commits f35c80e and f298e37; package tests and desktop/mobile browser checks passed.

milestones.title: Table filters match each field
milestones.outcome: Numeric, categorical, boolean, text, and date fields get suitable filters with visible row counts.
milestones.proof: Filters from the table update the summary and one existing chart, and reset restores all rows.
milestones.valid_intermediate_state: The package supports a complete single-source inspect-and-filter loop without host persistence.
milestones.rollback: Revert field-aware controls while retaining the shared profile and default inspection workspace.
milestones.proof_evidence: Commit 180089f; connected filters, single-filter removal, and clear all passed browser checks.

milestones.title: A host can save and restore the workspace
milestones.outcome: The public component emits serializable changes and accepts them again after remount.
milestones.proof: The demo host captures state, remounts with the same rows, and restores the same visible analysis.
milestones.valid_intermediate_state: The package is useful to the primary app and other React hosts without owning storage.
milestones.rollback: Remove the optional callback; savedData input and clipboard export continue to work.
milestones.proof_evidence: Commit 14e4f5e; callback tests passed. Browser restore kept 500 rows and two filters without an update loop.
